fields.name: Beginner
fields.description: Beginner climbing shoes are primarily designed for comfort and durability. These types of shoes often feature stiff midsoles, flat soles and low asymmetry (the shoe shape is usually closer to the natural shape of a foot). Unlike shoes for more experienced climbers, beginner shoes should fit comfortably without painful pressure points and will often be the same size as your street shoes. A proper fit means snug with no dead space, but never painful.

fields.name: Intermediate
fields.description:
Intermediate climbing shoes bridge the gap between comfortable beginner shoes and aggressive high-performance models. They feature a slightly downturned shape (moderate asymmetry) that helps grip small footholds and overhanging terrain, while still remaining comfortable enough for all-day climbing.

The midsole is stiffer than beginner shoes but softer than advanced models – offering a balance of support for edging and sensitivity for feeling the rock. Rubber typically ranges from 3.5mm to 4mm, providing better grip than entry-level shoes without sacrificing durability. Unlike beginner shoes (which fit like street shoes), intermediate shoes should fit snugly with toes curled – tight but not painful.

fields.name: Advanced
fields.description:
Expert climbing shoes are precision tools designed for maximum performance on demanding terrain. They feature an aggressive, downturned shape (high asymmetry) that concentrates power onto the big toe, allowing you to stand on microscopic edges and steep overhangs.

The midsole is minimal to nonexistent – prioritizing sensitivity and feel over comfort. Soft, sticky rubber (3–4mm) conforms to tiny features while providing exceptional friction on smears and slabs.

Fit is extremely tight and painful for many climbers. Toes are severely curled in a "crimped" position, with zero dead space. These shoes are typically removed between climbs due to discomfort.

fields.name: Bouldering
fields.description: Bouldering is a form of rock climbing performed on low walls (typically 10 to 15 feet tall) without the use of ropes or harnesses. Instead, climbers rely on thick crash pads for safety. The goal is to complete short but challenging sequences of moves called "problems." Bouldering emphasizes power, technique, and problem-solving, making it accessible to beginners and demanding for experts. Unlike traditional climbing, you don't need a partner or complex gear—just climbing shoes, a chalk bag, and determination.

fields.name: Outdoor
fields.description: Outdoor climbing is the real deal. There are no colored holds telling you where to go. You feel real rock—sharp, smooth, slimy, or juggy. Routes aren't "set" they're discovered. You'll deal with weather, bugs, dirt, and finding your own gear placements. It's less convenient but way more rewarding. Indoor climbing teaches you to move; outdoor climbing teaches you to read rock, manage fear, and connect with nature. Most climbers love both—they're just different adventures

fields.name: Top Rope
fields.description:
Top rope climbing is a style of rock climbing where the rope runs from the climber’s harness, up to a secure anchor at the top of the climb, and back down to a belayer on the ground. Because the rope is anchored overhead, if the climber falls or lets go, they will only drop a few inches before the rope catches them. This makes it the safest and most beginner-friendly form of roped climbing.

Unlike lead climbing, the climber does not clip the rope into the wall as they go up. The rope is already in place, so the climber can focus entirely on their footwork, balance, and technique rather than worrying about gear placement or taking big falls. Meanwhile, the belayer on the ground manages the slack and locks the rope instantly if the climber slips.

You will find top rope climbing at almost every indoor climbing gym, as well as at many outdoor crags where you can hike to the top to set up the anchors. It is an excellent tool for building endurance, practicing difficult moves repeatedly, and introducing new climbers to the sport. The main downsides are that you need easy access to the top of the cliff to set it up, and it lacks the intense mental adrenaline of lead climbing—but for pure movement practice and safety, nothing beats it.

fields.name: Sport Climbing
fields.description:
Sport climbing is a form of rock climbing in which the climber ascends a route protected by permanent bolts that have been drilled into the rock. The climber carries the rope up with them from the ground, attaching it to these fixed anchors at intervals as they move upward. This is done using quick draws—two carabiners connected by a sturdy piece of fabric—which clip into the bolt on one end and hold the rope on the other.

The route itself is defined by the spacing of these bolts, which are typically placed every few meters to offer reliable protection against falls. Because the climber is not attached to a rope suspended directly from the top, falling involves a longer drop past the last piece of protection they clipped. This dynamic aspect is an inherent part of the discipline, requiring the climber to manage their rope placement carefully and maintain focus on the sequence of moves ahead.

Sport climbing can be practised both indoors in climbing gyms and outdoors on natural rock faces. It is primarily a test of physical endurance, technique, and problem-solving, as routes are designed to challenge a climber's strength and agility through complex sequences of handholds and footholds. At a competitive level, athletes are judged on how high they can climb on a difficult route within a set time limit, making it as much a strategic mental game as a physical one.

fields.name: Traditional Climbing
fields.description:
Traditional climbing, often called "trad climbing," is a style of rock climbing where the climber places their own protective gear into the rock as they ascend, rather than clipping into pre-installed bolts. The climber carries a rack of removable devices—such as cams, nuts, and hexes—which are wedged into cracks and fissures in the rock. Each piece of gear is attached to the climber's harness via a carabiner, and the rope is clipped through these placements as the climber moves upward.

Because the protection is entirely dependent on the climber's judgement and placement skill, trad climbing carries a higher level of responsibility and risk than climbing on fixed bolts. A good placement can hold a significant fall, while a poor one can pop out under pressure. This requires a deep understanding of rock types, gear sizes, and body positioning to ensure each piece is seated securely.

The belayer on the ground manages the rope in the same way as in other roped styles, but must be especially attentive since falls can be unpredictable. Additionally, the climber must carefully manage their gear rack, choosing the right piece for each section of the crack or feature they encounter. This constant process of placing and removing protection makes trad climbing slower and more methodical, often described as a physical puzzle combined with a mental chess game.

Trad climbing is practised almost exclusively outdoors on natural rock, as indoor walls do not offer the cracks necessary for placing gear. It is the original form of roped climbing and remains popular for its adventurous spirit, self-reliance, and the deep connection it fosters with the natural environment.

fields.name: Lead Climbing
fields.description:
Lead climbing is a style of rock climbing where the climber attaches their rope to fixed bolts or removable gear as they ascend from the ground up. Unlike top-roping, the rope isn't already anchored above them—it trails below, and the climber's last clipped point is their only protection in a fall.

This creates higher risk. Because the climber must pull up slack to clip each piece of protection, a fall means dropping at least twice the distance to their last clip. This demands strong technique, good decision-making, and trust in your gear.

The belayer also plays a crucial role, managing slack carefully to protect the climber without hindering their movement. Lead climbing is more physically and mentally challenging than top-roping, but it's the standard for sport climbing and trad climbing, offering a truer sense of progression and adventure.

fields.name: Tarantula
fields.fit_notes: These climbing shoes feature forgiving leather that molds to your feet, so you don’t need to be a sizing expert to get a great fit. The flat, comfy design means no angry toes—just happy climbing, while the tough rubber won’t cry when you scrape it down the wall (we’ve all been there). A supportive platform keeps your arches thankful mid-session, and best of all, they’re wallet-friendly because great shoes shouldn’t require a second mortgage.

fields.name: Defy
fields.fit_notes: The Evolv Defy is a top-rated, entry-level climbing shoe designed for comfort and versatility, making the transition from rental shoes seamless and enjoyable. It features a neutral shape and a breathable synthetic upper that will not stretch over time, ensuring a consistent fit. The durable 4.2mm TRAX SAS rubber sole offers excellent grip, while the soft, supportive midsole provides enough rigidity for edging on small footholds. A padded split tongue and dual Velcro straps allow for easy on-and-off and a secure fit. Ideal for indoor climbing and bouldering, the Defy is a forgiving and dependable choice that supports beginners as they build confidence and progress.

fields.name: Jett S
fields.fit_notes: The Ocun Jett S is a soft, comfortable, and highly specialized gym slipper designed specifically for indoor bouldering. Its standout feature is a pointy, "dolphin-nose" toe that excels at hooking small pockets and digging into "innie" holds on steep terrain, while the unlined leather upper and single Velcro strap provide a sock-like, easy-on-off fit for high-volume sessions. The sensitive 4mm rubber and soft midsole allow excellent feel for volumes and smears on overhanging walls, though this same softness makes it less supportive for precise edging on outdoor rock. Overall, it's an ideal choice for intermediate climbers who primarily train indoors and want a forgiving, performance-oriented

fields.name: Arpia V
fields.fit_notes: The Scarpa Arpia V is a versatile, moderate-performance shoe built to bridge the gap between soft gym shoes and stiff outdoor performers, making it an ideal choice for the intermediate climber heading to the crag. Unlike overly aggressive bouldering shoes, it features a full-length midsole that provides the support and structure needed for edging on small, sharp outdoor footholds, while the moderate downturn still allows for confident climbing on vertical to slightly overhanging terrain. The 3.5mm Vibram XS Grip 2 rubber offers excellent friction on natural rock, and the dual Velcro straps ensure a secure, adjustable fit that remains comfortable for long days of sport or trad climbing.

fields.name: Ondra Comp
fields.fit_notes: The La Sportiva Ondra Comp is a revolutionary, high-performance bouldering shoe designed for expert climbers pushing their limits on steep terrain, competition-style problems, and training boards. Its most distinctive feature is a three-part sole with a soft, "gooey" central rubber pad that creates a dynamic, springy feel, allowing for explosive movement while still providing surprising edging power thanks to the 3.5mm Vibram XS Grip 2 outsole and 1.1mm LaSpoFlex midsole. The Ondra Comp delivers an unmatched blend of sensitivity, power, and precision for steep, technical bouldering at the highest level.

fields.name: Furia Air
fields.fit_notes: The Scarpa Furia Air is the ultimate expression of sensitivity in a climbing shoe, designed for expert climbers who prioritize surface feel and control over structural support. Weighing just 150 grams per shoe, this ultra-lightweight slipper features a double-layer perforated microfiber upper for breathability, an Alcantara insert under the big toe for enhanced tactile feedback, and a Vibram XS Grip 2 outsole that allows you to feel every micro-feature of the rock or volume. The 2026 update introduces a reinforced Velcro closure and a refined last for an even more precise, glove-like fit, while the extreme softness of the sole demands strong feet and advanced technique to unlock its full potential. Ideal for technical smearing, volume climbing indoors, and outdoor projects requiring maximum adaptability, the Furia Air is not for edging on vertical terrain or long routes—but for climbers who want to feel the rock like never before, it remains the benchmark in its class.

fields.title: How to Break in your Climbing Shoes
fields.description:
Breaking in a brand-new pair of climbing shoes is a delicate ritual that when done correctly can transforms stiff rubber and leather into a precision‑fit second skin. Conversely when done wrong, it can cut sessions short, ruin your skin, and even damage the shoe itself. It all starts before you even leave the store: leather shoes will stretch significantly, sometimes a full size, while synthetics hold their shape, so your benchmark should be a toe curl that feels uncomfortably tight when standing flat but never so agonising that you gasp and yank your foot out within a minute.

Once you have the right fit, resist the urge to take them straight to the wall. Instead, spend the first twenty‑four hours doing passive stretches at home, wearing thick cotton socks while walking around the house for short intervals. For unlined leather only, you can use a hairdryer on low heat to gently warm the toe box before flexing your foot until the material cools, but never apply heat to synthetic shoes because it will melt the glue.

When you finally hit the gym, adopt the three‑route rule: climb only three to five easy problems well below your grade, focusing on big, positive edges rather than tiny crystals or smears, because edging drives the toe box into the seams and speeds up the moulding. And you must take the shoes off the very second your feet touch the ground—never leave them on while belaying, as your feet swell and the sustained pressure creates hot spots and nerve compression.

If the shoes remain unbearably stiff after a few sessions, you can accelerate the process with the controversial but effective wet‑sock method. Put on thin liner socks, saturate them with warm water, put on the shoes, walk or climb gently for twenty minutes, then immediately stuff them with newspaper and let them dry for a full forty‑eight hours away from heat. This works only for leather, not synthetics, which will have their linings ruined.

Throughout the break‑in period, protect your skin by taping your big‑toe and pinky‑toe knuckles with zinc oxide tape before each session, as the internal stitching is abrasive. And never resort to commercial stretching sprays, because the alcohol they contain dries out the rubber and degrades the midsole, turning high‑performance shoes into floppy slippers within months.

Once you have logged about three sessions and the shoes feel seventy percent comfortable, force the arch to relax by down‑climbing slowly on a vertical wall. Place your heel low and push your toes deep into the front of the shoe, which stretches the heel rand backward and eases that dreaded dead‑toe feeling. Then, for the final push, do ten fast, easy boulder problems back‑to‑back—the rapid flexing generates internal heat and often marks the magic moment when the shoe finally surrenders to your foot.

Throughout this entire process, however, you must listen to your body and recognise the red lines: numbness, bruising under the toenails, or bleeding through the heel are never acceptable. If such pain persists beyond five sessions, you have simply bought the wrong shape for your foot, because no amount of suffering will turn a narrow last into a wide one.

In the end, a perfectly broken‑in climbing shoe should feel like a firm handshake—tight, secure, and supportive, without crushing—and should make no squeaking noise when you step, because that indicates dead air space. By session six, you should be able to wear them for an entire thirty‑minute warm‑up without the desperate urge to rip them off, and once you reach that point, they are truly yours, ready to perform at their best on every route you tackle.

fields.title: The UK's Best Outdoor Climbing Spots
fields.description:
The UK is a world-class climbing destination, offering an extraordinary variety of rock types and styles, from the rugged mountain crags of Scotland to the classic gritstone edges of the Peak District and the dramatic sea cliffs of Wales and the South West.

For those starting their outdoor journey or looking for accessible sport climbing, several quarries offer excellent bolted routes. For example Horseshoe Quarry in the Peak District is a hub for progression, with over 100 bolted routes, a strong concentration of moves in the V3 to V7 range, and easier climbs from V0 upwards on its Upper Tier. Similarly, Castle Inn Quarry in North Wales is an incredibly roadside-friendly spot with a great selection of slabby and off-vertical climbs with individual moves rated from V0 to V2, perfect for beginner leaders. The Wyndcliffe Quarry in the Wye Valley offers a peaceful woodland setting with a mix of sport and trad routes, with around a dozen sport routes featuring crux moves between V0 and V3. For a stunning coastal setting, the Southgate area on the Gower Peninsula is a "slabby winter paradise," with problems and route cruxes from V0 up to V12, though some crags are tidal and require careful planning. The Llanberis Pass offers enormous range of problems and routes on great rock, spanning from V0 on some lower angle slabs to V10 and beyond. The sea cliffs of Gogarth on Anglesey are legendary for serious climbers due to the high friction edges and striking crystal structures. Many of these Gogarth routes are tidal and under protection of the RSPB so some seasonal restrictions apply.

The spiritual home of British trad climbing is arguably the gritstone edges of the Peak District, such as the internationally renowned Stanage Edge and Curbar Edge, which offer a huge range of classic and often bold routes, with a long-standing ethic against bolting that preserves their traditional character. On these crags, you will find everything from easy solo traverses at VB to legendary test pieces with crux moves in the V8 to V10 range, and some of the hardest traditional routes in the country feature individual moves graded as high as V12 or V13. For a more adventurous mountain experience. 

Moving north, the Lake District presents a wealth of options for every type of climber, from the classic mountain routes on Dow Crag, which features 143 climbs with crux moves ranging from V0 to V9, to the testing sport climbs at Hodge Close Quarry with 81 routes that include bouldery V5 and V6 sequences. Dow Crag is a true mountain venue, offering a serious and exposed traditional climbing experience on its rhyolite rock, with classic multi-pitch routes like the 'C Ordinary Route' providing an excellent introduction to the grade, while harder test pieces like 'Eliminate A' push climbers to their limit. Meanwhile, the dramatic steep walls of Hodge Close Quarry present a completely different challenge, serving as the focal point for slate climbing in the region with a variety of well-bolted sport routes and more serious traditional lines. The quarry's easy access and quick-drying rock make it a favourite evening venue, with routes like the famously thin and technical E6 (7c+) test piece, Dogfight at Virgin Massacre Creek, showcasing the extreme end of the spectrum.

Scotland offers wild and rugged climbing, with spots like The Cobbler in the Trossachs, which provides a mix of classic routes and more severe climbs with cruxes spanning the entire V-grade spectrum from V0 to V10. The demanding high-grade trad routes on crags like Creag Tharsuinn near Loch Lomond, where some of the hardest lines feature individual moves in the V8 to V11 range. From the beginner-friendly slabs of the Wye Valley with moves at VB and V0, to the extreme V12 and V13 test pieces of the Peak District and the sea-cliff epics of Wales, the UK's outdoor climbing scene offers a lifetime of challenges for every climber.

fields.heading: BALANCE AND BODY POSITION
fields.description: Sticking one leg out to the side of your body (not on a foothold) to act as a counterbalance.
fields.example: You’d flag while climbing whenever you’re reaching with one hand on a steep overhang and feel your body starting to swing or "barndoor" away from the wall. For example, if your left hand is holding a good grip while your right hand reaches high, and both feet are directly under you, your body will naturally twist to the right. By taking your right foot off its hold and straightening that leg out to the side against the wall, you shift your center of gravity leftward, underneath your stable hand. This kills the swing, keeps your hips close to the wall, and gives you the balance needed to grab the next hold smoothly. In short: flag whenever a long reach makes you feel off-balance.

fields.heading: BALANCE AND BODY POSITION
fields.description: A barn door occurs when a climber's center of gravity shifts too far to one side while only two diagonal points of contact remain on the wall
fields.example: Holding a sidepull with the right hand while standing on a high right foothold, with the left hand and left foot both not on the a hold. In that position, the climber's body acts like a door swinging on a hinge, rotating outward and away from the wall. To prevent this, the climber must immediately counterbalance by flagging the free leg across the body or drop-kneeing to keep their hips close to the rock, otherwise the swing becomes unstoppable and they peel off.

fields.heading: FOOTWORK AND HANDHOLDS
fields.description: A small edge you grip with your fingertips, often with your thumb pressing over your index finger. These can be hard on the tendons so use with care

fields.heading: MOVEMENT AND TECHNIQUE
fields.description: A jump or lunge where both hands (or feet) leave the wall at once.

fields.heading: MOVEMENT AND TECHNIQUE
fields.description: Pressing down on a hold (like getting out of a swimming pool) to raise your body over it.

fields.heading: MOVEMENT AND TECHNIQUE
fields.description: Using one foot pulling (toe hook) and the other foot pushing (smear) on the same hold or feature.
